text: Everything in the last two lessons shared one property: the target never received a packet from you. Active reconnaissance is the opposite — the first moment traffic reaches infrastructure the target actually owns. That line isn't a technicality. It's the point where your signed Rules of Engagement stop being a formality and start being the only thing distinguishing you from an attacker, at least from the target's firewall logs.

A real engagement moves through this in order: confirm which hosts in an authorized range are actually alive, scan those hosts for open ports, then grab banners to confirm exactly what's listening. Each step sends a little more traffic than the last, and each one needs to stay strictly inside the IP ranges and time window the signed scope actually authorizes — none of that discipline applied to anything passive.

nmap dash s n ten dot twenty dot thirty dot zero slash twenty four runs a ping-style sweep with no ports touched at all — the lightest active technique available, used to narrow a large range down before deeper scanning. From there, nmap dash s capital S dash p dash against a single host runs a stealthy SYN scan across the full 1 through 65535 port range, rather than assuming unusual services only run on well-known ports.

An open port only proves a service exists. nc ten dot twenty dot thirty dot fifteen twenty two connects directly and reads whatever banner the service volunteers — OpenSSH 8.9, for example — a specific, versioned fact worth checking against known vulnerabilities later. Because active recon shows up in firewall logs and IDS alerts, real engagements throttle it with scan-delay or a slower T2 timing template, and never scan outside the allow-listed range.

That's the active side of reconnaissance: a ping sweep, a port scan, a banner grab, each one deliberate and scoped, never unthrottled. Next lesson, everything from both halves of this chapter — passive and active — gets synthesized into one structured attack surface map, the artifact that actually drives the scanning and enumeration work coming in Chapter 3.
